by_task.when: Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) are allowable and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) independently for every asset and include it even when a more specific federal exemption also applies. Its monetary ceiling limits protection but does not defeat EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not include § 522(d)(5) when federal subsection (d) exemptions are unavailable or the item is not the debtor's property.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general-property alternative, while retaining every applicable specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not include § 8123 for property outside the debtor's interest or when Pennsylvania law is not an allowable namespace.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) independently for the asset, without replacing applicable category-specific Oregon or federal exemptions.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply paragraph (p) to real property, property not belonging to the debtor, or a non-Oregon context.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent alternative for the asset, including when another subsection specifically covers its type.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply subsection (b) to business-use property, non-personal property, or property outside the debtor's ownership.

by_task.when: An asset matches an exemption's property and use category but the statute also states a dollar, aggregate, or item-count ceiling.
by_task.procedure: For EC, include the asset-law pairing if the law can protect any qualifying interest. Do not require the law to protect the asset's full value, and evaluate each asset as an eligible alternative rather than choosing a final allocation among competing assets.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not cite the law without the required property type, use, ownership, or other substantive eligibility facts; a ceiling cannot create category eligibility.

by_task.when: Considering a category-specific exemption rather than a general-property alternative.
by_task.procedure: Require the facts to satisfy that provision's stated property type and use. Federal § 522(d)(3) does not enumerate firearms; Arizona § 33-1125(1) and Pennsylvania § 8124(a)(1) require actual wearing apparel, not jewelry or firearms; Illinois § 12-1001(d) requires trade use and § 12-1001(e) requires a professionally prescribed health aid.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not transfer an exclusion to a different provision that expressly covers the item—for example, Oregon § 18.345(1)(b) expressly includes jewelry as well as wearing apparel. General-property alternatives remain independently available.

by_task.when: Arizona law applies to married debtors and Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1121 is being considered for an asset.
by_task.procedure: Use § 33-1121 only to understand that spouses may claim and combine article exemptions; do not return it as the asset's exemption citation. Return the operative property provision whose category the asset satisfies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not let this coordination rule remove an otherwise applicable Arizona property exemption or alter that provision's own married-couple limitation.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) are allowable and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate § 522(d)(5) independently for every asset and retain any applicable specific federal exemption. Report the protected amount for the whole asset as the lesser of its value and the available wildcard ceiling: $1,475 plus up to $13,950 unused under § 522(d)(1) for each debtor. Under § 522(m), the maximum is $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for two joint debtors when each has the full unused amount.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not include § 522(d)(5) when federal subsection (d) exemptions are unavailable or the asset is not debtor property. Do not omit it merely because a specific exemption also applies or treat its ceiling as a category test.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 independently in addition to every applicable specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption. For the whole asset, report the lesser of its value and $300 for one debtor, or $600 when two spouses jointly own it and each uses the statutory exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 8123 outside the debtor's property or a Pennsylvania namespace, and do not replace a qualifying specific exemption with this general alternative.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) independently and retain every applicable category-specific Oregon or federal alternative. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and $400; for this paragraph, do not double the asset-level output merely because two debtors jointly own the property.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply paragraph (p) to real property, property outside the debtor's ownership, or a non-Oregon context.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every such asset independently and retain applicable specific subsections. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and $4,000 for one debtor, or $8,000 for two joint debtors each entitled to the exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply subsection (b) to business-use property, non-personal property, property outside the debtor's ownership, or a non-Illinois context.

by_task.when: Considering an Illinois category-specific personal-property exemption.
by_task.procedure: Apply § 12-1001(a) to actual necessary wearing apparel and report the clothing's full value; apply subsection (d) only when facts establish use as a tool of the debtor's trade; apply subsection (e) only to a professionally prescribed health aid. Independently evaluate subsection (b) whenever its personal-use conditions hold.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel or ordinary household or office objects as tools of trade without stated trade use.

by_task.when: Considering an Arizona personal-item exemption for clothing or jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(1) only for actual wearing apparel, subject to its $500 ceiling. Section 33-1125(4) covers engagement and wedding rings, not jewelry generally.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, or other jewelry as wearing apparel, and do not infer a general Arizona jewelry exemption from the ring provision.

by_task.when: An independently eligible exemption states a dollar ceiling or is unlimited for the qualifying category.
by_task.procedure: Return the protected amount for the whole named asset. For a capped alternative, use the lesser of the asset's value and that alternative's applicable asset-level ceiling; for an uncapped alternative, use the asset's full value. In particular, § 522(d)(3) is limited to $700 per item despite its larger aggregate ceiling, and § 522(d)(4) never exceeds the jewelry's value. Combine debtor ceilings only when the particular provision permits it.
by_task.avoid_when: A ceiling does not establish category eligibility. Do not copy a ceiling when the asset is worth less, use an aggregate ceiling as a per-item amount, leave a half-interest as the final output, or double every ceiling merely because two debtors exist.

by_task.procedure: Evaluate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every such asset independently and retain applicable specific subsections. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and $4,000 for one debtor, or $8,000 for two joint debtors each entitled to the exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply subsection (b) to business-use property, non-personal property, property outside the debtor's ownership, or a non-Illinois context.

by_task.when: Considering an Illinois category-specific personal-property exemption.
by_task.procedure: Apply § 12-1001(a) to actual necessary wearing apparel and report the clothing's full value; apply subsection (d) only when facts establish use as a tool of the debtor's trade; apply subsection (e) only to a professionally prescribed health aid. Independently evaluate subsection (b) whenever its personal-use conditions hold.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel or ordinary household or office objects as tools of trade without stated trade use.

by_task.when: Considering an Arizona personal-item exemption for clothing or jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(1) only for actual wearing apparel, subject to its $500 ceiling. Section 33-1125(4) covers engagement and wedding rings, not jewelry generally.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, or other jewelry as wearing apparel, and do not infer a general Arizona jewelry exemption from the ring provision.

by_task.when: An independently eligible exemption states a dollar ceiling or is unlimited for the qualifying category.
by_task.procedure: Return the protected amount for the whole named asset. For a capped alternative, use the lesser of the asset's value and that alternative's applicable asset-level ceiling; for an uncapped alternative, use the asset's full value. In particular, § 522(d)(3) is limited to $700 per item despite its larger aggregate ceiling, and § 522(d)(4) never exceeds the jewelry's value. Combine debtor ceilings only when the particular provision permits it.
by_task.avoid_when: A ceiling does not establish category eligibility. Do not copy a ceiling when the asset is worth less, use an aggregate ceiling as a per-item amount, leave a half-interest as the final output, or double every ceiling merely because two debtors exist.
